Let's consider the vectors $\vvec=\twovec20$ and $\wvec=\twovec{-1}1$ as shown in [fig-span-linear-indep].

The vectors $\vvec$ and $\wvec$ and some linear combinations they create.

The figure shows us that $\bvec = \vvec + 2\wvec = \twovec02$ is a linear combination of $\vvec$ and $\wvec$. Indeed, we can verify this algebraically by constructing the linear system $$ \begin{bmatrix}\vvec \amp \wvec \end{bmatrix} ~ \xvec = \twovec02, $$ whose corresponding augmented matrix has the reduced row echelon form $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 2 \amp -1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array} \right] \sim \left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array} \right]. $$ Because this system is consistent, we know that $\bvec=\twovec02$ is in the span of $\vvec$ and $\wvec$.

In fact, we can say more. Notice that the coefficient matrix $$ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \amp -1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} $$ has a pivot position in every row. This means that for any other vector $\bvec$, the augmented matrix corresponding to the equation $\begin{bmatrix}\vvec \amp \wvec \end{bmatrix} ~\xvec = \bvec$ cannot have a pivot position in its rightmost column: $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 2 \amp -1 \amp * \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp * \\ \end{array} \right] \sim \left[ \begin{array}{rr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp * \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp * \\ \end{array} \right]. $$ Therefore, the equation $\begin{bmatrix}\vvec \amp \wvec \end{bmatrix} ~\xvec = \bvec$ is consistent for every two-dimensional vector $\bvec$, which tells us that every two-dimensional vector is in the span of $\vvec$ and $\wvec$. In this case, we say that the span of $\vvec$ and $\wvec$ is $\real^2$.

The intuitive meaning is that we can walk to any point in the plane by moving an appropriate distance in the $\vvec$ and $\wvec$ directions.
